title: Form or formless?
hookLine: love God with a face, or seek the reality beyond all faces? Arjuna asks which is better
carry: god with form or formless: both arrive

lines: A SMALL IMAGE, DRESSED AND FED.
cards: In one Hindu home there's a shrine with a small image of Krishna, dressed in real clothes, offered food, put to bed at night.

In another, someone sits in silence, eyes closed, and will tell you that God has no form at all, beyond every image and every name. Both are Hindu. And teachers have long disagreed about which comes closer.
Arjuna has just seen God in an overwhelming cosmic form, then in a gentle human one. So chapter twelve opens with the obvious next question.

teach.b: Verse one, Arjuna: some are always devoted to you, worshiping you. Others worship the imperishable, the unmanifest. Which of these knows yoga best?

teach.h: THOSE DEVOTED TO ME: MOST UNITED.
teach.b: Verse two, Krishna: those who fix their minds on me, always devoted, with the highest faith, I consider the most united.

But then verses three and four: those who worship the imperishable, which can't be described, the unmanifest, present everywhere, beyond thought, unchanging, unmoving, firm, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the good of all beings, they also reach me.
Both arrive. Verse five names the difference: the difficulty is greater for those whose minds are set on the unmanifest, because that path is hard for embodied beings. Beings with bodies love faces.
And verses six and seven: those who offer all their actions to me, and meditate on me with undivided devotion, I quickly lift out of the ocean of death and rebirth.
Hindus call these two roads saguna, God with qualities, and nirguna, God beyond them. Teachers read the passage differently.
In Advaita Vedanta, following Shankara, the formless is the final truth, and the path of form is the gentler road for many people.
In devotional schools, following teachers like Ramanuja, devotion to the personal Lord is itself the highest, and they read verse two that way.
Both readings keep what the text says: both arrive, and one road is harder. Form or formless?
Krishna's answer: both arrive. That's why one Hindu can dress a small Krishna in the morning and sit in silence at night.

how: Hindus worship God both with form (saguna), through images, names and stories, and as formless (nirguna), through silent meditation; many practice both, and chapter twelve is often read to honor each.

o: a god who hides from his worshipers
the unmanifest: what has no visible form
an empty void where nothing exists

games.q: what's inside the chapter — tap the pairs.
p: those devoted to me: most united

s: the Gita says those who seek the formless never arrive
verse 5 says the formless path is harder for embodied beings
the difficulty is greater for those whose minds are set on the unmanifest.
all Hindu schools agree on which path is highest
Advaita, following Shankara, holds the formless final; devotional schools, following Ramanuja and others, hold devotion to the personal Lord highest.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you ask which is better: worshiping God with a form, or the formless imperishable. what does Krishna say first?
o: those devoted to me with faith are the most united.
games.why: those fixed on him with devotion are most united. then he says the formless seekers also reach him, by a harder path.

practice: For one minute, picture a face or an image that feels sacred to you, a deity, a teacher, a loved one, a candle flame, and hold it with warmth.
For the next, let the image dissolve and rest in what's left: silence, space, awareness without a shape. Notice which feels closer today; there's no wrong answer, and the Gita says both arrive.

wordCard.voice: Avyakta, the unmanifest, what Krishna calls the formless beyond every image. Gita twelve: those devoted to God with a form, and those who seek the formless, both reach him; the formless path is harder for embodied beings.

orig.note: Sanskrit: avyakta, the unmanifest, the unseen; a (not) + vyakta (manifest, made visible).

carryVoice: Your line: God with form or formless, both arrive. A face, or the silence, and either can be the road. Day two hundred one, done.
